items.title: Swiss German diglossia
items.claim: German-speaking Switzerland uses Swiss German dialects for everyday speech and Standard German for which contexts?

options.text: Most writing, school instruction and formal broadcasting; daily speech remains dialect

items.reveal:
Linguists describe Swiss German as a textbook case of diglossia. Standard German is used for most written and formal contexts; dialect dominates speech, including on regional television.

Swiss German varieties differ substantially from one canton to another.
items.why: A community can run two registers of a language indefinitely in parallel.

items.title: Where German is spoken
items.claim: German is an official or co-official language of how many European countries?

options.text: Six (Germany, Austria, Switzerland, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, Belgium)

items.reveal_title: Six European states give German official status
items.reveal:
It is the sole official language in Liechtenstein and one of multiple in Belgium (East Cantons), Luxembourg, Switzerland and Italy's South Tyrol.

German is the most widely spoken native language in the EU (around 95 million).
items.why: Language geography rarely matches state borders neatly.

items.title: Klemperer's LTI
items.claim: Victor Klemperer's LTI: Notizbuch eines Philologen (1947) studied which subject?

options.text: The language of the Third Reich, observed during the war by a Romance philologist who survived persecution

items.reveal_title: A close linguistic analysis of Nazi-era German
items.reveal:
Klemperer (Romanist at Dresden, dismissed in 1935) compiled a study of Nazi-period vocabulary, rhetoric and propaganda forms.

The book has remained continuously in print as a model of linguistic study under dictatorship.
items.why: Documentary records of how a regime uses language can outlast the regime itself.
